title: Your Nitnem, for now
hookLine: a starter Nitnem is an invitation, not a test

cards: Two pieces of paper land on a desk. One is a test, face down, with a box for a grade. The other is a card, a name written on the envelope.
A daily prayer can look like the first: a full version you either pass or fail, so why start? Today ends ten days on Nitnem, and the point is the second piece of paper.
A starter Nitnem is closer to an invitation than a test.

teach.h: TEN DAYS OF THE DAILY BANIS.
teach.b: Look back at the ten days. Nitnem: the daily discipline, morning, evening, night. Japji Sahib, where Guru Nanak says clever thinking won't get you there.
Jaap Sahib's galloping praise of the Timeless. The savaiyas: without love, nothing. Chaupai: keep me.
Anand: joy, found. Rehras at dusk: put the day down. Sohila at night: the song for sleep.
And yesterday, the honest math. So what's a Nitnem for now? For Sikhs who have taken amrit, the full Nitnem is part of their vows, and they keep it.

teach.h: A VOW FOR SOME, A START FOR ALL.
teach.b: For everyone else on this path, whether a Sikh coming back to practice, someone learning alongside a Sikh partner, or someone simply curious, the Gurus' own words point to a gentler start.
Gurbani often calls the Guru's word amrit, nectar: something offered to drink.

teach.h: GUR PRASAD — BY THE GURU'S GRACE.
teach.b: And the Granth's very first lines, the Mul Mantar, end with two words: gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. In that reading, the invitation isn't earned. It's given.
So a starter Nitnem might be Japji's first pauri each morning, Sohila at night, or Anand's first stanza with your coffee.

teach.h: SAID DAILY, AT A REAL TIME.
teach.b: Whatever it is, it's said daily, at a time that already exists in your day.
And when a day slips, you do what you learned on the breath. You come back.

how: Amritdhari Sikhs keep the full Nitnem as part of their vows; many other Sikhs and newcomers begin with one bani said daily, such as Japji in the morning or Sohila at night, and add more over time.

o: the daily banis, begun with one, as you are
the full hour of prayer, done from day one
a test of devotion you pass or fail

games.q: ten days of Nitnem — tap the pairs.

s: the Mul Mantar ends with gur prasad, by the Guru's grace
the last words of the root verse.
for Sikhs who have taken amrit, Nitnem is optional
it's part of their vows; the gentler start is for everyone else on the path.
a starter Nitnem has to include every bani
one bani, said daily, is a real beginning.

games.q: you've chosen one bani, and on day three you miss it. what now?
o: come back tomorrow and say it again.
say it three times tomorrow to make up.
games.why: the same answer as simran on the breath: come back. steadiness, not a perfect score.

practice: Choose one morning bani, not forever, just for now: Japji's Mul Mantar and first pauri, Jaap's opening, one savaiya, Chaupai's first lines, or Anand's first stanza.
Picture tomorrow morning, where you'll be, how long it'll take, what you'll read or play; if you're here to learn rather than to pray, choose one to listen to. Then sit with the choice: it's made.

wordCard.voice: Your Nitnem. The daily banis, begun where you are: one bani, said every day, as an invitation, not a test.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: by the Guru's grace, the last words of the Mul Mantar.

carryVoice: Your line: one bani, daily. An invitation, not a test. Tomorrow, out of the house and somewhere new.
